It’s mostly late at night after work, when things quiet down. I’ll go through a whole pizza, a family-sized bag of chips, dessert—I don’t even taste a lot of it. It’s not hunger; it’s like a compulsion. I do it alone, locked up in my apartment because I’d be mortified if anyone saw. That part eats at me, no pun intended.

But it’s more than the eating. Lately, I’ve had these stretches—lasted over a week—where I barely sleep, maybe three hours a night, but I’m wired. I’m pacing, planning big ideas—starting a private security firm, launching a training program, stuff way beyond my current gig as a bodyguard. I feel unstoppable, like my brain’s moving faster than I can speak. People say I’m talking too fast, too loud. I’m not depressed—at least not during those times—just amped up, invincible. It’s when the energy finally crashes that I feel wrecked, but by then, I’ve already overspent, overcommitted. This has been going on for months.
D023-D008_h023.options:
A. Bipolar I Disorder
    B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation)
    C. Binge-Eating Disorder
    D. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

D023-D008_h024.question: I’ve been going through these intense periods where I can’t seem to sleep—like, three hours a night and I’m still wired. It started a few weeks ago after a big project wrapped up. I felt unstoppable: pitching three new films at once, barely sitting still, talking so fast my assistant asked if I was okay. That’s when the eating started. I’d order six meals at once, eat them all in my editing suite alone, past the point where I felt sick—just to quiet the race in my head. I knew it was too much, but everything felt urgent. I’d hide the deliveries, ashamed, like I was losing control even while feeling more alive than ever. But last week, the crash hit. I couldn’t get out of bed. Called in sick for the first time in years. I’ve had episodes like this before—after my divorce, actually—and the pattern’s familiar: the soaring highs, the reckless ideas, then the deep slumps. My therapist years ago mentioned mood swings, but this latest wave feels different because of how tightly the binges are tied to those manic surges—like they feed each other. It’s not just about food; it’s part of the bigger storm.
D023-D008_h024.options:
A. Bipolar I Disorder
    B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation)
    C. Binge-Eating Disorder
    D. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

D023-D008_h025.question:
I’ve been feeling overwhelmed lately, and it’s affecting everything. For the past three weeks, I’ve had these intense episodes where I eat so much in one sitting—whole pizzas, endless snacks, just nonstop—more than anyone should eat in a day, really. I keep doing it even when I’m painfully full, and I hide it, eating alone in my bedroom because I’m ashamed. My husband doesn’t even know the half of it.  

But it’s not just the eating. I haven’t slept more than two hours a night, and yet I’m full of energy—cleaning the house at 3 a.m., calling old colleagues to pitch wild ideas for a memoir or a travel blog, spending money on books and clothes I don’t need. I feel like my thoughts are racing, like I can’t keep up with myself. I’m not depressed; if anything, I feel powerful, like I don’t need rest.  

This isn’t new—these highs have happened before, even led to trouble a few years back when I maxed out our credit cards. But this time, the eating fits in, like it’s part of the storm. I know it’s not normal, but it all feels… justified in the moment.
D023-D008_h025.options:
A. Bipolar I Disorder
    B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation)
    C. Binge-Eating Disorder
    D. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
